analysis.one_liner: Requires big banks to stop financing fossil fuels and deforestation on a fixed timetable.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral, dying in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required US banks with $50 billion or more in assets to submit plans to the Federal Reserve for cutting their financing of fossil fuels: no new or expanded fossil fuel projects after 2023, no thermal coal financing after 2025, and no fossil fuel financing at all after 2030, with deforestation-risk financing phased out too [S2][S3]. Banks that failed to comply would face Federal Reserve penalties, including forced divestment of the offending assets [S3]. The bill also directed financial regulators to count a company's contribution to climate emissions when deciding how closely to supervise it [S2]. The bill never got a committee hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 117th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to climate change, especially low-income and minority communities that the bill said bear disproportionate harm from financed fossil fuel projects; energy-transition workers, whose retraining and severance the bill required banks to fund; and future generations, via the bill's hard deadline to stop financing new fossil fuel projects by 2023 and all fossil fuel financing by 2030 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities exposed to climate and pollution harms

how_it_helps.text: Requires large banks to submit plans to stop financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects by 2023, end thermal coal financing by 2025, and end all fossil fuel financing by 2030, with Federal Reserve approval and penalties including forced asset divestiture.

Banks' plans must prioritize withdrawing funding from companies that disproportionately harm low-income and minority communities and must include support for workers displaced by the energy transition, and plans may not count carbon offsets.

Adds climate contribution to the criteria regulators use to designate risky nonbank financial firms, and requires the Federal Reserve to report on financed emissions, the gaps in regulation, and the needs of workers and communities affected by the transition.

analysis.who_pays: Large US banks ($50B+ in assets), which would lose the ability to finance, underwrite, and trade fossil fuel assets; and fossil fuel companies, which would lose access to that financing on a fixed timeline [S3]. Some cost could pass through to consumers as financing for energy projects becomes scarcer or more expensive, and the bill acknowledged transition costs for fossil-fuel-dependent workers and communities [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks and fossil fuel companies

drawbacks.text: Cutting off bank financing for new fossil fuel projects by 2023 could raise energy costs or constrain fuel supply before clean alternatives are fully built out, a cost that falls on consumers — the bill contains no provisions addressing energy prices or supply.

The requirements apply only to US bank holding companies over $50 billion in assets; fossil fuel financing could migrate to foreign banks, private credit, or nonbank lenders, potentially reducing the bill's climate benefit while raising American companies' borrowing costs.

Opponents of restrictions on fossil fuel financing generally argue such rules limit capital for energy production; the bill also gives the Federal Reserve a central role in directing credit away from an entire industry, an unusual expansion of the central bank's remit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real problem — the largest banks finance the fossil fuel expansion driving climate change — with hard deadlines, Fed enforcement, and divestiture penalties, while explicitly requiring support for workers and communities hit by the transition and barring offsets. The strongest objection is that unilaterally cutting off American bank financing of fossil fuels could shift that financing to foreign banks and nonbank lenders with no climate standards, potentially raising energy costs at home while doing little for global emissions; banks and Republicans also argued it politicized the Fed. Its one-sided design (comprehensive climate constraints on banks, no supply-side energy planning) invited the charge that it was symbolic rather than a workable transition law. As introduced it was never tested in committee, so its real-world workability was never debated on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the Fossil Free Finance Act on November 4, 2021, with Senator Merkley joining as the bill's only cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and fossil fuel companies kept unrestricted access to US bank financing; the status quo was preserved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks and fossil fuel companies

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee, where it received no further action.

against.name: Banking industry groups
against.role: Major bank trade associations and the largest US banks
against.what_they_did: Opposed requirements to phase out fossil fuel financing, arguing banks should not be directed to cut off lending to an entire industry; such opposition was the prevailing view on the Senate Banking Committee, where the bill never received a hearing.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the bill's demise, which preserved bank financing for new and expanded fossil fuel projects.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats; with only 2 Senate Democrats or independents cosponsoring out of 50, and no Republicans, the bill had no visible bipartisan support and never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would bar these banks from financing new fossil fuel projects, then any fossil fuel financing, and require divestiture and Federal Reserve penalties for noncompliance — directly restricting a major lending and underwriting business line.
The industry's access to financing from large US banks would be cut off on a fixed timeline, raising its cost of capital and blocking expansion of new projects, pipelines, and terminals.

industries.industry: Clean energy and negative-emissions technology firms
industries.note: As bank capital retreated from fossil fuels, lending could shift toward non-fossil energy and proven carbon-removal projects, which the bill explicitly allows to count toward targets (offsets do not).
